name: The Pointers to Polaris
summary: The first hop almost everyone learns: two stars at the front of the Big Dipper point to Polaris, the star that marks north and barely moves all night.
steps: Find the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]] and pick out the two stars on the front edge of the bowl, the side away from the handle: [[star:Merak|Merak]] at the bottom and [[star:Dubhe|Dubhe]] at the rim. They are about three fingers (5°) apart.
Run a line from Merak through Dubhe, out of the open top of the bowl, and carry it on for about five times that gap, roughly one outstretched hand span (29°).
The first moderately bright star you meet, standing fairly alone, is [[star:Polaris|Polaris]]. The line misses it by about two degrees, which is close enough.
Check: Polaris is the end of the faint [[asterism:little-dipper|Little Dipper]] handle, and its height above your horizon equals your latitude.

name: Arc to Arcturus, speed on to Spica
summary: The curve of the Big Dipper's handle leads to two of the brightest stars of the spring sky, orange Arcturus and blue-white Spica.
steps: Start at the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]]'s handle: [[star:Alioth|Alioth]], [[star:Mizar|Mizar]] and [[star:Alkaid|Alkaid]] make a gentle curve about a fist (11°) long.
Keep that curve going away from the bowl for about one outstretched hand span (31°) to the brightest star in that part of the sky, orange [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]].
Carry the same curve on for about another hand span (33°) to [[star:Spica|Spica]], a single bright blue-white star lower down.
Say it as you go: arc to Arcturus, speed on to Spica. The whole sweep is about 75°, nearly halfway across the sky.

name: Orion's Belt to Sirius
summary: The three stars of Orion's Belt point to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, and the hop works from almost anywhere on Earth.
steps: Find [[asterism:orions-belt|Orion's Belt]], three evenly spaced stars in a short straight row about two fingers (3°) long: [[star:Mintaka|Mintaka]], [[star:Alnilam|Alnilam]] and [[star:Alnitak|Alnitak]].
Follow the row from Mintaka through Alnitak and keep going for about eight Belt-lengths, a little over two fists (22°).
You land on [[star:Sirius|Sirius]], far brighter than any other star nearby. When it is low it often twinkles in flashes of color.

name: Orion's Belt to Aldebaran and the Pleiades
summary: The Belt pointed the other way leads to orange Aldebaran, the eye of Taurus, and on to the Pleiades, the best-known star cluster in the sky.
steps: Find [[asterism:orions-belt|Orion's Belt]] and this time follow it the other way, from [[star:Alnitak|Alnitak]] through [[star:Mintaka|Mintaka]], away from Sirius.
About two fists (22°) along, a little off the line, is [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]], a bright orange star at the tip of a V of fainter stars.
Carry on in roughly the same direction for another fist and a half (14°) to [[dso:M45|the Pleiades]], a tiny misty cluster shaped like a very small dipper.

name: The Southern Cross to the south celestial pole
summary: There is no bright star at the south celestial pole, so southern observers use the long bar of the Southern Cross to find south instead.
steps: Find the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]] and its long bar, from [[star:Gacrux|Gacrux]] at the top to [[star:Acrux|Acrux]] at the foot, about three fingers (6°) long.
Extend that bar past Acrux, away from Gacrux, for about four and a half times its length, one outstretched hand span (27°).
That spot, empty of bright stars, is the [[point:scp|south celestial pole]]. Drop straight down from it to the horizon and you are facing due south.
To check, draw a line halfway between the two [[star:Rigil Kentaurus|Pointers]] at right angles to them; it should cross the Cross's line within a few degrees of the same spot.

name: The leaky Dipper to Regulus
summary: Poke a hole in the bottom of the Big Dipper's bowl and the water drips onto Leo, landing near Regulus, the lion's heart.
steps: In the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]]'s bowl, use the two stars nearest the handle: [[star:Megrez|Megrez]], where the handle joins, and [[star:Phecda|Phecda]] below it, about three fingers (4°) apart.
Run a line from Megrez through Phecda, out through the bottom of the bowl, and keep going for about five fists (47°).
You reach [[star:Regulus|Regulus]], the bright star at the foot of a backward question mark of stars, the [[asterism:sickle-of-leo|Sickle]] of Leo.

name: Cassiopeia to the Andromeda Galaxy
summary: The W of Cassiopeia gives a quick arrow to the Andromeda Galaxy, the most distant thing most people will ever see with their own eyes.
steps: Find [[asterism:cassiopeia-w|Cassiopeia's W]] and look at the half of it that includes [[star:Caph|Caph]], [[star:Schedar|Schedar]] and the middle star [[star:γ Cas|γ Cassiopeiae]]. Schedar is the point of that V.
From γ Cas through Schedar, then on in the direction the point of the V aims, go about a fist and a half (15°) toward the Great Square.
Look for a faint elongated smudge: [[dso:M31|M31]]. It is easier if you look slightly to one side of it; binoculars show its bright oval core.

name: The Pointers to the Southern Cross
summary: Alpha and Beta Centauri point the way to the Southern Cross and tell it apart from the larger, dimmer False Cross nearby.
steps: Find the two brilliant stars close together low in the Milky Way: [[star:Rigil Kentaurus|Alpha Centauri]] (the brighter, yellowish one) and [[star:Hadar|Hadar]] (Beta Centauri), about three fingers (4°) apart.
Run a line from Alpha Centauri through Hadar and carry it on for about a fist (12°).
It arrives at the top of the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]], [[star:Gacrux|Gacrux]], a reddish star. A cross with no bright pointers beside it is the False Cross.

name: The Summer Triangle
summary: Three bright stars in three constellations make a big triangle that anchors the whole July to October sky and frames the Milky Way.
steps: Start at [[star:Vega|Vega]], the brightest of the three, a bluish-white star.
About one outstretched hand span (24°) away, in the Milky Way, is [[star:Deneb|Deneb]], the tail of the swan and the top of the [[asterism:northern-cross|Northern Cross]].
From Deneb go about one long hand span (38°) to [[star:Altair|Altair]], recognizable by a fainter star close on each side of it.
Altair back to Vega closes the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]] (34°). The Milky Way runs through the triangle, between Vega and Altair.

name: The Big Dipper to Castor and Pollux
summary: A diagonal across the Big Dipper's bowl leads to the Gemini twins, a matched pair of bright stars that is easy to confirm once you arrive.
steps: Draw a diagonal across the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]]'s bowl from [[star:Megrez|Megrez]], where the handle joins, to [[star:Merak|Merak]], the opposite corner, about a fist (10°).
Carry the line on out of the bowl for about four fists (43°) to [[star:Castor|Castor]], which sits almost exactly on it.
Just three fingers (4.5°) from Castor is [[star:Pollux|Pollux]], a little brighter and more orange. Two similar stars this close together confirm you have the twins.

name: Orion's shoulders to Procyon
summary: The line across Orion's shoulders leads to Procyon, the third corner of the Winter Triangle with Betelgeuse and Sirius.
steps: Find Orion's two shoulder stars: white [[star:Bellatrix|Bellatrix]] and orange-red [[star:Betelgeuse|Betelgeuse]], about three fingers (8°) apart.
Run a line from Bellatrix through Betelgeuse and continue about one outstretched hand span (26°), away from Orion.
The bright star there is [[star:Procyon|Procyon]]. With Betelgeuse and [[star:Sirius|Sirius]] it makes the [[asterism:winter-triangle|Winter Triangle]], almost equal-sided.

name: The Great Square to the Andromeda Galaxy
summary: The classic route to M31: walk along Andromeda's chain of stars from the corner of the Great Square, then turn and climb two steps.
steps: Start at [[star:Alpheratz|Alpheratz]], the corner of the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]] that also belongs to Andromeda.
Follow the chain of stars that leads away from the Square: [[star:δ And|δ Andromedae]] about three fingers (7°) along, then [[star:Mirach|Mirach]] about a fist (8°) farther.
At Mirach turn sharply toward Cassiopeia and step two fingers (4°) to the fainter [[star:μ And|μ Andromedae]].
The same step again brings you to [[dso:M31|the Andromeda Galaxy]], a soft oval glow, best seen with averted vision or binoculars.

name: The Great Square to Fomalhaut
summary: The west side of the Great Square points to Fomalhaut, the lone bright star of the autumn sky, in an otherwise faint region.
steps: Find the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]] and its western side, the one farther from Andromeda: [[star:Scheat|Scheat]] at its northern end and [[star:Markab|Markab]] at its southern end, about a fist (13°) apart.
Run a line from Scheat through Markab and keep going, away from the Square, for about four fists (45°).
The only bright star in that area is [[star:Fomalhaut|Fomalhaut]], in Piscis Austrinus. From mid-northern latitudes it never climbs very high.

name: The Pleiades to the Hyades and Aldebaran
summary: From the Pleiades a short hop leads to the V-shaped Hyades, the nearest big star cluster, with bright Aldebaran sitting in front of it.
steps: Find [[dso:M45|the Pleiades]], the small misty dipper of stars, and look about a fist (12°) away toward Orion.
There is a V of fairly bright stars a few fingers across: the [[dso:Mel25|Hyades]] cluster, the face of Taurus the bull.
Bright orange [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]] marks the end of one arm of the V, two fingers (2°) from the cluster's center. It is not a member: it is less than half as far away as the Hyades.

name: Orion to Capella
summary: A line up through Orion's head leads to Capella, the bright yellowish star that crowns the winter sky for northern observers.
steps: Start at [[star:Alnilam|Alnilam]], the middle star of [[asterism:orions-belt|Orion's Belt]], and find Orion's head, the faint small knot of stars led by [[star:Meissa|Meissa]], about a fist (11°) away between the shoulders.
Carry the line from Alnilam through Meissa on, away from the Belt, for about one long hand span (36°).
The brilliant star you reach is [[star:Capella|Capella]] in Auriga. A small triangle of fainter stars, the Kids, sits just beside it.

name: Vega to Albireo
summary: Albireo, the foot of the Northern Cross, is one of the prettiest double stars in a small telescope, and it is easy to reach from Vega.
steps: Start at [[star:Vega|Vega]] and look toward [[star:Altair|Altair]], the far corner of the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]].
A little less than halfway there, about a fist and a half (16°) from Vega and slightly off the line, is a modest star alone in the Milky Way: [[star:Albireo|Albireo]].

Check it with the [[asterism:northern-cross|Northern Cross]]: the long bar from [[star:Deneb|Deneb]] through [[star:Sadr|Sadr]] ends at Albireo. A small telescope splits it into a gold star and a blue one.

name: Antares to the Teapot and the center of the galaxy
summary: From red Antares a hop east reaches the Teapot of Sagittarius, whose spout points to the direction of the center of our galaxy.
steps: Find [[star:Antares|Antares]], the red heart of Scorpius, and follow the Milky Way east from it for about two and a half fists (25°).
You reach the [[asterism:teapot|Teapot]] of Sagittarius. Its spout is a narrow triangle; [[star:Kaus Media|Kaus Media]] is at its base and [[star:Alnasl|Alnasl]] is the tip, three fingers (3°) away.

The spout points back toward Scorpius. About three fingers (5°) past its tip lies the [[radec:266.417,-29.008|direction of the galactic center]], hidden behind dust, where the Milky Way's star clouds look thickest.

name: Sirius to Canopus
summary: Canopus, the second-brightest star of the night, lies almost due south of Sirius and is a key signpost for southern observers.
steps: Find [[star:Sirius|Sirius]], using [[asterism:orions-belt|Orion's Belt]] if you need to.
From Sirius go almost due south, toward the south celestial pole, for about three and a half fists (36°).
The brilliant white star there is [[star:Canopus|Canopus]]. It never rises for observers north of about 37°N, and it never sets for observers south of about 37°S.

name: Arcturus to the Hercules Cluster
summary: From Arcturus a three-step hop through Corona Borealis to the Keystone of Hercules finds M13, the best globular star cluster in the northern sky.
steps: From [[star:Arcturus|Arcturus]] go about two fists (20°) to [[star:Alphecca|Alphecca]], the bright gem in the small semicircle of Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown.
Continue in nearly the same direction for a fist and a half (15°) to [[star:ζ Her|ζ Herculis]], one corner of the [[asterism:keystone|Keystone]], a lopsided square of four modest stars.
Along the Keystone's side from ζ to [[star:η Her|η Herculis]], about two-thirds of the way, is [[dso:M13|M13]], a faint fuzzy star to the eye in dark skies and a round glow in binoculars.

name: Cassiopeia to the Double Cluster and Perseus
summary: Two stars of Cassiopeia point to the Double Cluster, a pair of star clusters side by side, and on to Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus.
steps: Find [[asterism:cassiopeia-w|Cassiopeia's W]] on the opposite side of [[star:Polaris|Polaris]] from the Big Dipper. Use the middle star [[star:γ Cas|γ Cassiopeiae]] and its neighbor [[star:Ruchbah|Ruchbah]], about two fingers (4°) apart.
Run a line from γ Cas through Ruchbah and keep going about three fingers (8°), twice their gap.
There you should see a small hazy patch in the Milky Way. Binoculars turn it into two rich clusters side by side: [[dso:NGC869|h]] and [[dso:NGC884|χ Persei]], the Double Cluster.
About a fist (12°) farther on is [[star:Mirfak|Mirfak]], the brightest star of Perseus, set in a loose group of stars that looks lovely in binoculars.

name: Corvus to Spica
summary: The small four-sided figure of Corvus, the crow, points to Spica, a second way to Virgo's brightest star that works well from both hemispheres.
steps: Find Corvus, a compact lopsided four-sided figure of stars of similar brightness, and its upper side, the one nearer Spica, from [[star:Gienah|Gienah]] to [[star:Algorab|Algorab]], about two fingers (3.5°).
Run a line from Gienah through Algorab and continue about a fist and a half (15°).
You arrive at [[star:Spica|Spica]], the bright blue-white star of Virgo.

name: The Great Square to Polaris
summary: On autumn evenings, when the Big Dipper sits low, the eastern side of the Great Square points through Cassiopeia straight to Polaris.
steps: Find the [[asterism:great-square|Great Square of Pegasus]] and its eastern side: [[star:Algenib|Algenib]] at its southern end and [[star:Alpheratz|Alpheratz]] at its northern end, about a fist and a half (14°) apart.
Run a line from Algenib through Alpheratz and on for about three fists (30°) to [[star:Caph|Caph]], the end star of [[asterism:cassiopeia-w|Cassiopeia's W]].
Keep the same line going another three fists (30°) to [[star:Polaris|Polaris]], which this line hits almost dead on.

name: Leo to the Coma Star Cluster
summary: Past Leo's tail lies Coma Berenices, a wide loose cluster of faint stars that is a fine test of a dark sky and a pair of binoculars.
steps: Start at [[star:Regulus|Regulus]] and follow Leo's body to the tail star [[star:Denebola|Denebola]], about one outstretched hand span (25°) away.
Carry on past Denebola for about a fist and a half (14°), bending a little to the side nearer the Big Dipper.
In a dark sky you will see a sprinkle of faint stars spread over several fingers: the [[dso:Mel111|Coma Star Cluster]], Berenice's Hair. Binoculars frame it well.

name: Scorpius's stinger to M7 and M6
summary: The close pair of stars at the tip of Scorpius's tail points to two bright open star clusters, M7 and M6.
steps: Follow the curved tail of Scorpius to its end, where two stars sit very close together: [[star:Shaula|Shaula]] and [[star:Lesath|Lesath]], less than a finger (0.6°) apart.
From Lesath through Shaula, look on toward the Teapot about three fingers (5°). A hazy patch there is [[dso:M7|M7]], which binoculars show as a big scatter of stars.
About two fingers (4°) from M7, on the side toward Antares, is the smaller [[dso:M6|M6]], the Butterfly Cluster.
From mid-northern latitudes the stinger never climbs much above 10° to 13°, so you need a clear, dark southern horizon; from mid-southern latitudes it passes high overhead.

name: The Southern Cross to the Coalsack and the Jewel Box
summary: Two contrasting sights inside the Southern Cross: a dark cloud of dust that blots out the Milky Way, and a sparkling cluster of colorful stars.
steps: Find the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]] and its brightest star, [[star:Acrux|Acrux]], at the foot.

Right beside Acrux, on the eastern side of the Cross (the side [[star:Mimosa|Mimosa]] is on), the Milky Way has a dark, almost starless hole several fingers across: the [[dso:C99|Coalsack]], a cloud of dust in front of the stars.

Go to Mimosa, the bright star at the eastern end of the crossbar. Just a little-finger width (1°) from it is a fuzzy star that binoculars or a small telescope reveal as the [[dso:NGC4755|Jewel Box]] cluster.

name: Canopus to Achernar
summary: Achernar, the bright end of the river Eridanus, completes the set of signposts around the south celestial pole with Canopus and the Southern Cross.
steps: Start at [[star:Canopus|Canopus]], the brilliant star south of [[star:Sirius|Sirius]].
Go about four fists (39°) away from Sirius's side of the sky, keeping about the same distance from the [[point:scp|south celestial pole]], to the next bright star, [[star:Achernar|Achernar]].
Check: Achernar and the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]] sit on roughly opposite sides of the south celestial pole, so when one is high the other is low.

name: Altair to Delphinus and Sagitta
summary: Two small but charming constellations sit right beside Altair: the dolphin Delphinus and the arrow Sagitta.
steps: Start at [[star:Altair|Altair]], the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]] corner with a fainter star on each side.
Look about a fist (10°) north of Altair, toward [[star:Albireo|Albireo]], for a short slim line of faint stars: Sagitta, the arrow, with [[star:δ Sge|δ Sagittae]] near its middle.
Now look east of Altair, about a fist (13°) away, for a tight little diamond of stars with a tail: Delphinus, the dolphin. [[star:Rotanev|Rotanev]] is the diamond's nearest corner to Altair.
